Add compound index on branch_versions(version_id, branch_name) (#871)

This index dramatically improves query performance when filtering
verifications from the provider's main branch. Without this index,
the query performs ~330M row comparisons, taking ~13.5 seconds.
With the index, execution time drops to ~6.5ms (~2,000x faster).

The index addresses the TODO comment in verification.rb:38 and
follows the existing migration pattern for compound indexes.

Fixes #872

chore: drop branch_versions_branch_name_index (#894)

* chore: branch_versions_branch_name_index prevents branch_versions_version_id_branch_name_idx from being used by the PG query planner. This appears safe to remove.

fix: avoid N+1 cascade

This eagerly loads data, thereby avoiding an N+1 cascade. The unit tests
show a reduction in the number of SQL queries from ~400 to ~20. Testing
in our dev environment also showed a 10x decrease in the response.

The only concern with this change is that this may result in too much
data being eagerly loaded. Having said that:

- The data is required _at some point_ anyway, otherwise, it wouldn't be
  fetching all the data. A sequential loading may mean that less data is
  handled at any one time though.
- All endpoints which use this decorator are impacted by the same N+1
  cascade, so this change will not result in excessive data in endpoints
  which may not need it.

Signed-off-by: JP-Ellis <josh@jpellis.me>

The previous change to eager loading seems to have introduced an

feat: Optimize WIP Query Performance to Prevent Timeouts on Large Datasets (#902)

* feat: Optimize WIP Query Performance to Prevent Timeouts on Large Datasets

Problem: WIP pact queries timing out on large datasets due to unbounded lookback windows and inefficient table scans.

Solution:

Add database indexes on verifications(provider_id, provider_version_id, success, wip, pact_version_id) and pact_publications(provider_id, created_at)
Constrain queries to last 30 days of verification activity using new config verified_by_other_branch_before_this_branch_look_back
Filter by verifications.execution_date instead of versions.created_at to avoid unnecessary joins and correctly identify recent branch activity
Optimize for_all_tag_heads to pre-filter consumers before aggregating tags
Configuration:

New env var: PACT_BROKER_VERIFIED_BY_OTHER_BRANCH_LOOKBACK_DAYS (default: 30)
Impact: Reduces query scope and leverages indexes to prevent cartesian explosion on providers with many old branches/verifications.

fix: use cvpv when checking can-i-deploy against an environment (#903) (#934)

When an application uses record-release, multiple provider versions can
be simultaneously live in the same environment. The previous cvp latestby
collapsed these down to the latest provider version, hiding incompatible
versions that were still live and producing false "deployable: true" results.

Switch to cvpv for all can-i-deploy paths that target an environment so
that every co-resident released or deployed version is evaluated
independently. The cvp default is preserved for tag-based and non-environment
queries where collapsing to the latest is correct.

Co-authored-by: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

chore(deps): update postgres docker digest to 3a82e1f

perf(matrix): flatten selector union to prevent quadratic query nesting

ids_for_selectors reduced its per-selector datasets with Sequel's union,
whose from_self default rewraps the entire accumulated dataset in a new
subquery on every step. With N selectors the query nested N-1 layers of
"SELECT * FROM (...)", and the matrix / can-i-deploy query infers one
selector per integrated pacticipant. A hub application with hundreds of
integrations produced hundreds of stacked subqueries for the database to
plan, bringing it to a halt.

Pass from_self: false so the selectors compose into a single flat UNION.
The individual selector arms carry no ORDER BY or LIMIT, so no wrapping is
needed to preserve their semantics.

Assisted-by: Claude Code:claude-opus-4-8[1m]

test(matrix): make the query baseline reproducible enough to diff

The baseline exists so two runs can be compared, but almost every line of the
generated file changed between runs of unchanged code, leaving nothing a diff
could tell you. Four things drifted.

Surrogate keys are embedded as literals in the captured SQL, and the suite
clears tables by deleting rows, which does not rewind a sequence; ids therefore
started wherever the previous run stopped. The rows left behind also bloated
the heap, so page counts, scan costs and buffer counts crept up on every run.
Truncating with RESTART IDENTITY and vacuuming fixes both, at the cost of the
generator having to own its database state rather than run inside the suite's
transaction.

Pact content came from a helper that embeds a random number, which varied the
stored row lengths and so the pages the matrix queries touched. Keying the
content on the pact's own identity keeps every pact distinct while making the
bytes on disk the same each time.

Plans were captured with wall-clock timings, which vary with unrelated machine
load and swamped what little signal survived. Ask Postgres for the work done —
costs, row counts, buffers, memory — and not for how fast this machine did it.

Vacuuming also gathers the statistics the planner was missing. Without them it
was estimating 300 rows against an actual 73 and choosing plans on guesses,
and whether autovacuum had run by then was a race.

Two further corrections to what the baseline measures. Every pact ended on a
passing verification, because the counter driving the alternation advanced
twice per call and so never changed parity; half of them now end on a failure,
which is what gives can-i-deploy a failure path to profile. Branch, tag and
ignore selectors were never exercised at all, so a regression in resolving them
would not have shown up.

The generator now fails and names the offending statements if any EXPLAIN
fails, rather than passing as long as a single one anywhere succeeded, and
each EXPLAIN runs in its own transaction so a failure cannot abort the run and
blame a later shape.

fix(matrix): honour use_case_sensitive_resource_names when resolving selectors

use_case_sensitive_resource_names was honoured on some matrix selector
paths and ignored on others: SelectorResolver matched pacticipant names
exactly, while Version.where_pacticipant_name went through the
case-insensitive name_like helper. An operator who turned the flag off
to get case-insensitive pacticipant names got them on some requests and
not others, depending on which internal path handled the lookup.

SelectorResolver now honours the flag too, so matrix and can-i-deploy
requests behave consistently regardless of which path resolves the
selector. Requests that name a pacticipant in a different case than it
is stored now resolve where they previously did not, which is the
intended correction.

Matching case-insensitively means a name can match more than one
pacticipant, which an exact match could never do. Rather than resolve to
an arbitrary one of them and answer can-i-deploy for the wrong service,
this reuses the error the pacticipant repository already raises for the
same situation, which names the duplicates and how to resolve them.

The default (case-sensitive) behaviour is unchanged, since name_like
collapses to an exact match in that mode.

perf(matrix): filter matrix rows by the already-resolved version ids

The matrix query resolved its selectors twice. SelectorResolver turns
every selector into concrete version ids before the query runs, and the
query then discarded them and re-derived the same ids in SQL, building
one union arm per selector with its own pacticipant and environment name
lookups. For can-i-deploy against an environment for a service with
thirty integrations, that is roughly a hundred and twenty union arms and
twice as many redundant name lookups in a single statement.

Both dataset methods now filter on the ids the resolver already
produced. Selectors that specify a version filter on the version id;
name-only selectors carry no version id, so they filter on the
pacticipant instead. That identifies the same rows, because a pact
publication's consumer id is the pacticipant id of its consumer version.

The two kinds have to be partitioned rather than handled uniformly,
because the callers that match a selector against either side of an
integration pass their selectors unfiltered. Filtering a name-only
selector on a version id would render an empty predicate and silently
return an empty matrix.

Query count per request is unchanged: selector resolution already ran as
its own statement, so this removes work from within a statement rather
than a round trip.

chore: add git-cliff config and the release script

The release script replaces the bump and conventional-changelog gems as the
source of the next version and the changelog entry: prepare computes the next
version, prepends the changelog, force-pushes the release branch and opens or
updates a draft PR whose body is the pending changelog entry; tag reads the
version back from the file prepare wrote, so the two agree by construction;
increment reports the bump size for the gem-released dispatch payload.

--dry-run against real history is how prepare and tag are checked, since a
run against the actual repository exercises the same git and gh calls a real
release would make.

Sets RUST_LOG=error: git-cliff logs INFO/WARN to stderr regardless of TTY, and
run/run! capture stdout and stderr together, so uncontrolled logging would
corrupt the captured version string and changelog body. error rather than
off, since run! builds CommandError entirely from that same merged output,
and a genuine git-cliff failure must still surface its ERROR-level
diagnostics.

next_version runs git-cliff through run!, so a non-zero exit raises rather
than being parsed. git-cliff prints the current version and exits 0 when there
is nothing to bump, so only a genuine failure is non-zero, and a broken
configuration cannot be mistaken for an empty release.

chore(ci): release the gem by merging a pull request

prepare keeps a draft "chore: release vX.Y.Z" pull request from the
release/pact_broker branch current with every push to master, computing the
next version and changelog entry with git-cliff. build verifies the gemspec
on that PR before any tag exists. Merging the PR pushes the vX.Y.Z tag, which
publishes the gem to RubyGems via OIDC trusted publishing, creates the GitHub
release, and dispatches gem-released with the same payload release_gem.yml
sent, so trigger_pact_docs_update.yml and pact-broker-docker are unaffected.

tag reads the version from the pull request's merge commit rather than
master's HEAD at checkout time, so a PR merged after the release PR can't
land above the tag and vanish from the next changelog. publish guards against
a hand-pushed tag by failing loudly when the tag disagrees with
lib/pact_broker/version.rb, pushes the gem before creating the GitHub
release so a failed push can't leave a release for a gem that never
published, and extracts the changelog entry by matching only the "## "
version headings that git-cliff and this repository's history now share, so
a git-cliff group heading can't be mistaken for the start of the next
release and truncate the body.

Removes script/release.sh, script/trigger-release.sh,
script/release-via-github-action.sh, tasks/release.rake and release_gem.yml,
along with the bump and conventional-changelog gems. The remaining ways to
cut a release are the pull request and, as an escape hatch, pushing the tag

docs: describe the pull request release process

Releases are made by merging a pull request rather than by running a script
locally. Every push to master updates a draft pull request from the
release/pact_broker branch with the next version and the changelog entry
computed from conventional commits since the last tag; reviewing that pull
request is how the changelog gets reviewed. Merging it pushes the version
tag, which publishes the gem, creates the GitHub release and notifies
pact-broker-docker. A hand-pushed tag remains as an escape hatch for when the
normal path is broken.

Publishing depends on a trusted publisher configured on rubygems.org and on
the rubygems GitHub environment existing, neither of which is visible from
the workflow file alone. Recording the prerequisite here points an on-call
maintainer at the right place when the OIDC step fails.

fix: pass JSON.parse options as keywords for json 3

json 3.0.0 changed every option on JSON.parse and JSON.load into a
keyword argument. A positional options hash now raises
`ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (given 2, expected 1)`, and an
unrecognised keyword raises instead of being ignored. Both hit the
broker as soon as the gem resolves to 3.x: the example-data seeder fails
on boot, and every pact publication returns 500 from
`PactBroker::Pacts::Parse`.

The broker's own CI never sees this because the `approvals` test gem
pins `json ~> 2.0`. The pact-broker-docker image installs without the
test group, so its lockfile maintenance picked up json 3.0.2 and
surfaced the breakage.

Changes, each valid on json 2.19.9 (the gemspec floor) and on 3.x:

- Splat `PACT_PARSING_OPTIONS` at every call site.
- Drop `create_additions: false`. json 3 removed the option; `JSON.parse`
  never enabled it on 2.x either.
- Add `allow_duplicate_key: true`. json 3 rejects duplicate keys by
  default; this keeps the last-key-wins behaviour that 2.x applied so a
  pact that published before json 3 still publishes after.
- Replace `JSON.load` in `CreateFormattedDiff` with `JSON.parse`. On 2.x
  `JSON.load` defaulted to `create_additions: true`, which is why the
  call passed the option explicitly; `JSON.parse` has no such default, so
  the option is no longer needed. Both inputs are pact strings read from
  the database, so `JSON.load`'s nil handling was unused.
- Drop `quirks_mode: true` from the HTML renderer. json 2 ignored it;
  json 3 raises on it.
